newsitem.title: italy: Zaire force contributors to review troop needs.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force contributors to review troop needs.

text.p: South Africa said on Sunday countries sending troops to eastern Zaire would meet this week in Germany to review the force's size and mandate now that hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees are going home.

Deputy President Thabu Mbeki told a news conference at the World Food Summit that South Africa agreed with other African countries that the terms of the multinational mission needed to be changed as a result.

His comments also reflected dissatisfaction among Africans with the way the U.N.-sponsored force had been organised and came amid other indications, including from the United States, that the operation might be rethought.
Representatives for troop contributors, including South Africa, would meet in the German city of Stuttgart, where the U.S.'s military European command is located, on Wednesday to discuss the issue.

The announcement came as hundreds of thousands of refugees made their way back to Rwanda and the first Canadians in a U.N. multinational intervention force arrived in the Rwandan capital, Kigali to prepare for the arrival of the rest of the force.

Mbeki said the Canadian-led force, which may number up to 10,000 troops, should "be decided by the nature of the problem". The United Nations has said the force is still needed to help deliver humanitarian aid in the central African region.
"We do not need the sort of numbers that have been spoken of in the past," Mbeki said.
Leaders of some countries from Africa's Great Lake region met at the Rome summit on Saturday.

"One of the decisions that they took, with which we agree, was that in light of the movement of refugees into Rwanda it will be necessary to review the mandate of that multinational force," Mbeki said.

"We will then, of course, take advantage of that (Stuttgart meeting)...to have some assessment of how many refugees remain in Zaire and then what kind of response is required to deal with whoever might be remaining," he said.
"But I think one of the urgent questions that remains is that you've got these refugees who might have shifted location and are now in Rwanda and who still need to be fed and clothed," Mbeki said.
Rwandan Prime Minister Pierre Celestine Rwigema told the summit on Saturday that the force should be scrapped, and its budget spent instead on re-settling the refugees in his country.
Burundi's Prime Minister Pascale Firmin Ndimira said the force was needed but suggested it be more actively involved in bringing the refugees home and not simply help with aid.
Kenya and other African countries have complained that they were not consulted properly before the U.N. Security Council approved the force last week.
